extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning elementary/topology (advanced undergraduates, beginning graduate students, general mathematically-inclined readers)
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory textbook chapter presenting fundamental concepts and theorems of topology (Euler's formula for polyhedra, topological transformations, connectivity, Jordan curve theorem, four-color problem, concept of dimension, Brouwer fixed-point theorem) with definitions, examples, and proof sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron is a solid whose surface consists of a number of polygonal faces. In the case of the regular solids, all the polygons are congruent and all the angles at vertices are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to distinguish regular polyhedra (Platonic solids) and to set up counting relations among vertices, edges, and faces for further theorems (e.g., Euler's formula and classification of regular polyhedra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron is simple if there are no 'holes' in it, so that its surface can be deformed continuously into the surface of a sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 is asserted to hold for simple polyhedra; non-simple polyhedra (with holes) do not satisfy the formula without modification. The notion is geometric/topological (deformability to a sphere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's formula for polyhedra
rubrics_metrics.description: In a simple polyhedron let V denote the number of vertices, E the number of edges, and F the number of faces; then always V - E + F = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: remove one face and flatten the remaining surface to a plane network (so the missing face reduces F by 1), triangulate by adding diagonals (each diagonal increases E and F by 1 so V - E + F unchanged), then iteratively remove boundary triangles by two types of deletions that preserve V - E + F, ending with a single triangle (V - E + F = 1) for the plane network, hence V - E + F = 2 for the original polyhedron. Emphasizes triangulation and boundary-triangle removal as invariant-preserving operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation and invariant-preserving operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangulate plane networks by drawing diagonals (increases both E and F by 1, preserving V - E + F). Remove boundary triangles of two types; each removal keeps V - E + F unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific operations are the constructive maneuvers in the proof of Euler's formula and illustrate the method of reducing a complex network to a simple base case while preserving the invariant V - E + F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting relations for regular polyhedra (nF = 2E, rV = 2E) and classification constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: For a regular polyhedron with F faces each n-sided and r edges meeting at each vertex: nF = 2E and rV = 2E. Combined with V - E + F = 2 these give algebraic constraints that limit possible (n, r) and hence yield only five regular polyhedra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these equalities to derive equation (4) in the text and classify possible values of n and r (e.g., n>3, r>3 cannot both hold) to obtain the Platonic solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological transformation (homeomorphism) — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological transformation of a figure A into A' is a correspondence between points p of A and p' of A' that is (1) biunique (one-to-one and onto) and (2) continuous in both directions (continuous mapping and inverse continuous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes intuitive examples: deformations of a rubber sheet (stretching, twisting without tearing or identifying distinct points) and more general operations like cutting and sewing (if sewn in the same way) which can still define topological transformations though not deformations. Emphasizes that topological transformations preserve topological properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological property (invariance under topological transformations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any property of a geometrical figure A that holds for every figure obtainable from A by a topological transformation is called a topological property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: connectivity, Euler characteristic, dimension. Metric or projective quantities (lengths, angles, areas, cross-ratios) are not topological properties. Intuition often guides but rigorous definition is required for generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connectivity: simply connected, multiply connected, n-tuply connected
rubrics_metrics.description: A planar domain is simply connected if every closed curve in the domain can be continuously shrunk to a point within the domain. A domain that is not simply connected is multiply connected. If n - 1 non-intersecting cuts from boundary to boundary are needed to convert a domain into a simply connected domain, it is n-tuply connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connectivity (degree of connectivity) is an important topological invariant. Examples: disk interior is simply connected; annulus between two concentric circles is doubly connected and becomes simply connected after one cut along a radius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jordan Curve Theorem (informal statement and necessity of precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple closed curve C in the plane divides the plane into exactly two domains — an inside and an outside — such that points in the same class can be joined without crossing C and points in different classes cannot be joined without crossing C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although obvious for polygons or smooth curves, the theorem is nontrivial for arbitrary simple closed curves (topological images of a circle). Jordan's original proof had gaps; rigorous proofs are subtle and historically important. The text notes it's simple to prove for polygons and promises a polygonal proof in the appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four Color Problem (map coloring) — statement and adjacency definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture: For any subdivision of the plane into non-overlapping regions, it is always possible to color the regions with four colors so that no two adjacent regions (regions sharing a whole segment of boundary) have the same color. Regions meeting only at points are not considered adjacent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical notes: proofs for restricted cases, Kempe's flawed proof, Heawood's five-color theorem (five colors suffice) and the conjecture remains a major problem (proved for maps with fewer than 38 regions; equivalence of plane and sphere by removing a face). Emphasizes precise definition of adjacency (segment vs point contact) and regularization of boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of dimension — inductive/recursive definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Dimension is defined inductively: define dimension -1 as the empty set; a set is dimension 0 if each point can be enclosed in arbitrarily small regions whose boundary intersects the set in a set of dimension -1; in general, a set S has dimension n if it is not of any lower dimension and each point of S can be enclosed in arbitrarily small regions whose boundary intersects S in a set of dimension n - 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: finite sets and the Cantor set are dimension 0; a line segment is dimension 1; plane is dimension 2; Cartesian n-space has dimension n. The definition matches Euclidean notions and resolves subtle examples like the Cantor set and rational points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiling theorem (Lebesgue-Brouwer) as characterization of dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: If an n-dimensional figure is covered by sufficiently small subregions, then there will exist points belonging to at least n + 1 of these subregions; moreover, it is possible to find a covering by arbitrarily small regions for which no point belongs to more than n + 1 subregions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'tiling' property characterizes n-dimensionality and can be taken as an alternative/characteristic definition of dimension. Examples: in 2D coverings there are points where three regions meet; in 3D there are points where four regions meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance of dimensionality
rubrics_metrics.description: The dimension of any set is a topological feature of the set; no two figures of different dimensions can be topologically equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underlines that dimension (as defined) is preserved under homeomorphisms, and contrasts with cardinality facts (e.g., line and square have same cardinality but are not topologically equivalent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem (disk version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any continuous transformation of a closed disk into itself (points remain within the circle) leaves at least one point fixed: there exists a point whose image equals itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch given: assume no fixed point, attach vectors PP' to each point, analyze the index (algebraic net rotation) of boundary vectors (index = +1), show index must be same on concentric inner circles by continuity, but for a sufficiently small circle index would be 0 — contradiction. The theorem generalizes to any region homeomorphic to a disk and has a three-dimensional analog (proof more difficult). Emphasizes use of vector/ index arguments and continuity.
